title: Moran Proposes a Film Tax Credit. What Would East Texas Get?
seoTitle: Moran’s Film Tax Credit: What East Texas Can Check
seoDescription: Moran’s federal film-credit bill remains in committee. Read its rural rules, compare Texas’s existing grant program, and track the local benefits claimed.
thumbnailMessage: Proposed film credit. Where would the money go?
summary: Moran’s September 24 film and television tax-credit bill remains referred to committee. Its rural rules are specific, and Texas already runs a separate grant program. Here is what residents can check before treating promised jobs as results.
content:
Nathaniel Moran has introduced a federal film and television tax-credit proposal that gives East Texas a concrete Washington record to follow. It does not yet give a local production company a new credit to claim.

H.R. 10582, the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, was introduced September 24, 2026. The official bill-status file, updated October 2, still lists referral to the House Ways and Means Committee as its latest action. It records no House passage, Senate passage or enactment.

## What the proposal would pay for

The introduced text would create a credit starting at 20 percent of qualified compensation, with specified increases capped at 30 percent. That is a percentage of qualifying compensation, not an automatic rebate on the entire production budget.

For the main film-and-television category, the text requires a commercial feature film, television pilot or television season costing more than $1 million, with 75 percent of principal-photography days in the United States. Separate rules address visual effects and post-production. News, advertising and productions intended primarily for social-media platforms are among the exclusions.

The provision aimed most directly at rural communities would add five percentage points when at least 30 percent of principal-photography days occur in a qualifying rural Opportunity Zone, or when the separate disaster-area conditions are met. Filming somewhere rural would not, by itself, satisfy the Opportunity Zone requirement. The proposed effective date concerns principal photography beginning in taxable years after December 31, 2026. Those provisions could change before passage.

## The East Texas promise needs a local record

In his September 24 announcement, Moran says productions can bring spending to caterers, hotels, hardware stores and tradespeople. He argues the federal incentive would help keep production work in the United States. The release describes a bipartisan House group and companion Senate legislation.

Those are the sponsor's stated goals. They do not establish that a production has selected East Texas, that a local employer will add a particular number of jobs, or that the proposed credit will pay for itself. No district-specific jobs or revenue estimate is represented in this article.

## Texas already has a separate grant program

The Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program is an existing state program. The Texas Film Commission describes it as a cash grant, rather than a state income-tax credit. An accepted application still must satisfy the program's requirements and complete expenditure review before a payment is made.

Its current film-and-television guide lists grants up to 31 percent of eligible Texas spending. Minimum conditions include $250,000 in eligible Texas spending, at least 60 percent of production completed in Texas, and separate 35-percent residency requirements for paid cast and paid crew. Applications must arrive before principal photography begins; starting production does not create eligibility retroactively.

The federal proposal and the Texas program have different qualifying rules and different payment bases. Adding their advertised percentages does not establish the benefit for a particular project.

## What to watch next

The next useful federal record is committee action, revised text or a recorded vote on H.R. 10582. A sponsor's announcement is a starting point for that review.

For local accountability, ask which East Texas productions receive awards, how much eligible spending they document, and how many Texas jobs they report. The Film Commission's impact page links a paid-project list through August 31, 2026, updated in September. That provides an existing record to examine while Congress considers the new proposal.

Record check: October 2, 2026, Central time. This article reports a pending proposal and an existing state program; it makes no endorsement or claim of guaranteed local benefit.
